assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix integers m >= 2 and g >= 0. Translate multiplicity-m numerical semigroups of genus g into Kunz-coordinate tuples with coordinate sum g; this gives N(m,g) = |K_{m,g}|. Do the same for genus g+1 to get N(m,g+1) = |K_{m,g+1}|. Next, prove separately that K_{m,g} and K_{m,g+1} are finite. Then invoke the core combinatorial lemma asserting the existence of an injective map J_{m,g} : K_{m,g} -> K_{m,g+1}. By the finite-set injection principle, this implies |K_{m,g}| <= |K_{m,g+1}|. Finally, substitute the two counting equalities to obtain N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1). This assembly explicitly fixes the earlier gap: finiteness is established before the cardinality comparison is made, and no use is made of the previously rejected false 'least admissible coordinate' injection.

steps.derives: For every integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, N(m,g) = |K_{m,g}|, where K_{m,g} is the set of positive integer tuples satisfying the multiplicity-m Kunz inequalities and having coordinate sum g.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the statement of L3.

steps.derives: For every integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, the set K_{m,g} is finite.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the statement of L4 with the given parameters m and g.

steps.derives: For every integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, the set K_{m,g+1} is finite.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L4 with the same m and with genus parameter replaced by g+1. Since g >= 0, we have g+1 >= 0, so the lemma applies.

steps.derives: For every integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, there exists an injective function J_{m,g} : K_{m,g} -> K_{m,g+1}.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the statement of L5.

steps.derives: For every integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, |K_{m,g}| <= |K_{m,g+1}|.
steps.trivial_justification: From A2, the set K_{m,g} is finite. From A3, the set K_{m,g+1} is finite. From A4, there exists an injective function J_{m,g} from K_{m,g} to K_{m,g+1}. Applying L6 to A = K_{m,g}, B = K_{m,g+1}, and f = J_{m,g} yields |K_{m,g}| <= |K_{m,g+1}|.

steps.derives: For every integer m >= 2 and every integer g >= 0, the number N(m,g) of numerical semigroups with multiplicity m and genus g satisfies N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1).
steps.trivial_justification: Apply A1 with genus g to obtain N(m,g) = |K_{m,g}|. Apply A1 again with genus g+1 to obtain N(m,g+1) = |K_{m,g+1}|. From A5 we have |K_{m,g}| <= |K_{m,g+1}|. Substituting the two equalities into this inequality gives N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1), which is exactly the root theorem statement.

shared_context.content: A numerical semigroup is a subset S of the nonnegative integers N0 such that 0 belongs to S, S is closed under addition, and N0 \ S is finite. The multiplicity of S is the least positive element of S. The genus of S is the cardinality of N0 \ S.
shared_context.label: Numerical semigroup

shared_context.content: For integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, N(m,g) denotes the number of numerical semigroups whose multiplicity is m and whose genus is g.
shared_context.label: Counting function N(m,g)

decomposition.strategy_summary: Use the Kunz-coordinate encoding only to translate the theorem into a finite combinatorial counting problem, but unlike the rejected attempt, do not use the false 'least admissible coordinate' map. Instead, isolate the genus-raising step as a separate existence-of-injection lemma on Kunz vectors, and add explicit finiteness lemmas before applying the finite-set injection principle.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix an integer m>=2.

We prove both directions.

Forward direction. Let S be a numerical semigroup of multiplicity m. Thus S\subseteq N_0, 0\in S, S is closed under addition, N_0\setminus S is finite, and the least positive element of S is m.

For each i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, define w_i to be the least element of S congruent to i modulo m. We first justify existence of w_i. Since N_0\setminus S is finite, there exists some integer N such that every n\ge N lies in S. Fix i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}. Choose q so large that qm+i\ge N. Then qm+i\in S and qm+i\equiv i\pmod m. Hence the set \{s\in S:s\equiv i\pmod m\} is nonempty, so its least element w_i exists.

By definition w_i\equiv i\pmod m, so there is an integer x_i with w_i=mx_i+i.

We now show x_i is a positive integer. Since w_i\in S and w_i\equiv i\not\equiv 0\pmod m, we have w_i\ne 0. Therefore w_i is a positive element of S. Because m is the multiplicity of S, every positive element of S is at least m, so w_i\ge m. If x_i\le 0, then w_i=mx_i+i\le i<m, contradicting w_i\ge m. Hence x_i\ge 1. Therefore each x_i is a positive integer.

Next we prove the stated description of S:
S = {0} \cup \{qm:q\in N_0\} \cup \{qm+(mx_i+i): q\in N_0, 1\le i\le m-1\}.

First, every element of the right-hand side belongs to S. Indeed, 0\in S. Also m\in S, so by closure under addition qm\in S for every q\in N_0. And since w_i=mx_i+i\in S, again by closure qm+w_i\in S for every q\in N_0. Thus the right-hand side is contained in S.

Conversely, let s\in S. If s=0, then s is in the right-hand side. If s>0 and s\equiv 0\pmod m, write s=qm with q\in N_0; then s is in the right-hand side. If s\equiv i\pmod m for some i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, then by minimality of w_i among elements of S in that residue class we have s\ge w_i, and since s-w_i is divisible by m we may write s=w_i+qm for some integer q\ge 0. Hence s=qm+(mx_i+i), so again s lies in the right-hand side. This proves equality.

Now we prove the Kunz inequalities.

Take i,j\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}.

Case 1: i+j<m. Then w_i+w_j\in S by closure, and
w_i+w_j \equiv i+j \pmod m.
Since w_{i+j} is the least element of S congruent to i+j mod m, we get
w_i+w_j\ge w_{i+j}.
Substituting w_t=mx_t+t gives
(mx_i+i)+(mx_j+j) \ge mx_{i+j}+(i+j),
so
m(x_i+x_j)\ge mx_{i+j}.
Because m>0, this yields x_i+x_j\ge x_{i+j}.

Case 2: i+j>m. Then w_i+w_j\in S and
w_i+w_j \equiv i+j-m \pmod m,
with i+j-m\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}. By minimality of w_{i+j-m},
w_i+w_j\ge w_{i+j-m}.
Substituting gives
(mx_i+i)+(mx_j+j) \ge mx_{i+j-m}+(i+j-m),
that is,
m(x_i+x_j+1)\ge mx_{i+j-m}.
Hence x_i+x_j+1\ge x_{i+j-m}.

This proves all assertions in the forward direction.

Converse direction. Now let x=(x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}) be any tuple of positive integers satisfying:
- if i+j<m, then x_i+x_j\ge x_{i+j};
- if i+j>m, then x_i+x_j+1\ge x_{i+j-m};
for all i,j\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}.

Define
S_x := {0} \cup \{qm:q\in N_0\} \cup \{qm+(mx_i+i): q\in N_0,\ 1\le i\le m-1\}.
We must show S_x is a numerical semigroup of multiplicity m.

First, S_x\subseteq N_0 and 0\in S_x by definition.

Second, m\in S_x (take q=1 in \{qm:q\in N_0\}). Also, no positive integer less than m belongs to S_x. Indeed, every nonzero multiple qm of m is at least m, and every element of the third set has the form
qm+(mx_i+i)=m(q+x_i)+i.
Since x_i\ge 1 and q\ge 0, we have q+x_i\ge 1, so this number is at least m+i>m. Therefore the least positive element of S_x is m, once we know S_x is a numerical semigroup. In particular, multiplicity m will follow.

Third, N_0\setminus S_x is finite. For each residue class i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, all numbers congruent to i mod m and at least mx_i+i belong to S_x, because they are exactly the numbers qm+(mx_i+i) with q\in N_0. Also every multiple of m belongs to S_x. Thus the only possible missing numbers are:
- no multiples of m are missing;
- in residue class i, only the finitely many numbers i, m+i, 2m+i, ..., (x_i-1)m+i may be missing.
Hence N_0\setminus S_x is finite.

It remains to prove closure under addition. Let a,b\in S_x. We consider cases.

1. If a=0 or b=0, then a+b is the other summand, so a+b\in S_x.

2. If both a and b are multiples of m, say a=q_1m and b=q_2m, then a+b=(q_1+q_2)m\in S_x.

3. If one is a multiple of m and the other is not, say a=q_1m and b=q_2m+(mx_i+i) for some i, then
a+b=(q_1+q_2)m+(mx_i+i)\in S_x.
The same argument applies with a and b interchanged.

4. Suppose both are of the third type:
a=q_1m+(mx_i+i),\qquad b=q_2m+(mx_j+j)
for some i,j\in\{1,\dots,m-1\} and q_1,q_2\in N_0.
Then
a+b=(q_1+q_2)m + (mx_i+i)+(mx_j+j).
We split according to i+j.

4a. If i+j<m, then by the inequality x_i+x_j\ge x_{i+j}. Hence there exists an integer
r:=x_i+x_j-x_{i+j}\ge 0.
Now
(mx_i+i)+(mx_j+j)=m(x_i+x_j)+(i+j)=mr+(mx_{i+j}+(i+j)).
Therefore
a+b=(q_1+q_2+r)m + (mx_{i+j}+(i+j)) \in S_x.

4b. If i+j=m, then
(mx_i+i)+(mx_j+j)=m(x_i+x_j+1),
so
a+b=(q_1+q_2+x_i+x_j+1)m\in S_x.

4c. If i+j>m, then by the inequality x_i+x_j+1\ge x_{i+j-m}. Hence
r:=x_i+x_j+1-x_{i+j-m}\ge 0.
Also
(mx_i+i)+(mx_j+j)=m(x_i+x_j)+i+j = mr + (mx_{i+j-m}+(i+j-m)).
Indeed, since i+j=(i+j-m)+m,
m(x_i+x_j)+i+j = m(x_i+x_j+1)+(i+j-m)
= mr + (mx_{i+j-m}+(i+j-m)).
Thus
a+b=(q_1+q_2+r)m + (mx_{i+j-m}+(i+j-m)) \in S_x.

In all cases a+b\in S_x, so S_x is closed under addition.

We have shown that S_x is a subset of N_0 containing 0, closed under addition, and with finite complement in N_0. Therefore S_x is a numerical semigroup. Since m\in S_x and no positive integer less than m belongs to S_x, its multiplicity is exactly m.

This proves the converse.

Therefore, for every integer m\ge 2, the numerical semigroups of multiplicity m are exactly those obtained from positive integer tuples (x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}) satisfying the stated Kunz inequalities, via the displayed formula, and for a given numerical semigroup the associated coordinates satisfy all the asserted properties.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2. For a numerical semigroup S of multiplicity m, define for each i in {1,2,...,m-1} the Apéry representative w_i to be the least element of S congruent to i modulo m, and write w_i = m x_i + i with x_i an integer. Then each x_i is a positive integer, the set S is exactly {0} union {q m : q in N0} union {q m + (m x_i + i) : q in N0 and 1 <= i <= m-1}, and the tuple x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) satisfies the Kunz inequalities: for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}. Conversely, if x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) is any tuple of positive integers satisfying those same Kunz inequalities, and S_x is defined by S_x = {0} union {q m : q in N0} union {q m + (m x_i + i) : q in N0 and 1 <= i <= m-1}, then S_x is a numerical semigroup of multiplicity m.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix an integer m >= 2 and a tuple x=(x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers satisfying the stated Kunz inequalities, and define

S_x = {0} ∪ {q m : q ∈ N0} ∪ {q m + (m x_i + i) : q ∈ N0, 1 <= i <= m-1}.

We must prove that the genus g(S_x), i.e. the number of elements of N0 \ S_x, is

sum_{i=1}^{m-1} x_i.

The proof is by describing exactly which nonnegative integers are missing from S_x.

First, every nonnegative integer n has a unique expression n = q m + r with q ∈ N0 and 0 <= r <= m-1.

We analyze membership in S_x residue class by residue class modulo m.

1. Residue class 0 modulo m.
If r=0, then n=q m, so by definition n ∈ S_x. Hence there are no gaps in the residue class 0 modulo m.

2. Residue class i modulo m, where 1 <= i <= m-1.
Take n = q m + i with q ∈ N0.

We claim:

n ∈ S_x if and only if q >= x_i.

Indeed, by definition, the elements of S_x congruent to i mod m are exactly those of the form

q' m + (m x_i + i) = (q' + x_i)m + i

with q' ∈ N0. Thus the set of elements of S_x having residue i mod m is exactly

{t m + i : t >= x_i, t ∈ N0}.

So for n=q m+i we have n ∈ S_x exactly when q >= x_i, proving the claim.

Therefore the elements of N0 in residue class i that are not in S_x are precisely

i, m+i, 2m+i, ..., (x_i-1)m+i.

Because x_i is a positive integer, this list contains exactly x_i numbers.

3. Counting all gaps.
By the preceding analysis, the gaps of S_x are exactly the union over i=1,...,m-1 of the sets

{i, m+i, 2m+i, ..., (x_i-1)m+i}.

These sets are pairwise disjoint, because their elements have different residues modulo m. Hence the total number of gaps is the sum of their cardinalities:

|N0 \ S_x| = sum_{i=1}^{m-1} x_i.

By definition of genus, g(S_x) = |N0 \ S_x|. Therefore

g(S_x) = sum_{i=1}^{m-1} x_i.

This is exactly the desired conclusion.

Note that the Kunz inequalities were not needed for this counting argument itself; they serve to ensure that the set defined from x is indeed a numerical semigroup in the intended correspondence. Once S_x is given by the displayed formula, the genus is determined by the above residue-class count.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix integers m\ge 2 and g\ge 0. We prove that the numerical semigroups of multiplicity m and genus g are in bijection with the set K_{m,g}.

We use the standard definitions.
A numerical semigroup is a cofinite submonoid S of \mathbb N_0 containing 0. Its multiplicity is its least positive element, denoted m(S). Its genus is g(S):=|\mathbb N_0\setminus S|. For a nonzero m\in S, the Apéry set of S with respect to m is
Ap(S,m):=\{w\in S: w-m\notin S\}.
It is standard and easy to check that Ap(S,m) contains exactly one element in each residue class mod m; thus we may write
Ap(S,m)=\{w_0,w_1,\dots,w_{m-1}\}
with w_0=0 and w_i\equiv i\pmod m for 1\le i\le m-1.
Since m is the multiplicity, no positive integer <m belongs to S, hence for i=1,\dots,m-1 we have w_i>i. Therefore each w_i has the form
w_i=i+m x_i
with x_i\in \mathbb Z_{>0}.
The tuple x=(x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}) is the Kunz-coordinate vector of S.

We first show that if S has multiplicity m and genus g, then its Kunz-coordinate vector lies in K_{m,g}.

Let S be a numerical semigroup with multiplicity m and genus g. Define x_i by w_i=i+m x_i as above.

1. Positivity.
For each i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, we have x_i\ge 1 because w_i>i.

2. Kunz inequalities.
Take any i,j\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}.
Because w_i,w_j\in S and S is closed under addition, w_i+w_j\in S.

If i+j<m, then w_i+w_j\equiv i+j\pmod m. Since w_{i+j} is the least element of S congruent to i+j mod m, we have
w_i+w_j\ge w_{i+j}.
Substituting w_k=k+m x_k gives
(i+m x_i)+(j+m x_j)\ge (i+j)+m x_{i+j},
so m(x_i+x_j)\ge m x_{i+j}, hence
x_i+x_j\ge x_{i+j}.

If i+j>m, then w_i+w_j\equiv i+j-m\pmod m. Again by minimality of the Apéry representative in that residue class,
w_i+w_j\ge w_{i+j-m}.
Substituting,
(i+m x_i)+(j+m x_j)\ge (i+j-m)+m x_{i+j-m}.
Since i+j=(i+j-m)+m, this becomes
m(x_i+x_j+1)\ge m x_{i+j-m},
so
x_i+x_j+1\ge x_{i+j-m}.
Thus all required inequalities hold.

3. Sum equals genus.
For each residue class i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, the numbers congruent to i mod m that are smaller than w_i are exactly
i,\ i+m,\ i+2m,\ \dots,\ i+(x_i-1)m,
and there are exactly x_i of them. By definition of w_i as the least element of S in that residue class, all these x_i numbers are gaps of S. Conversely, every gap of S is of this form for a unique residue class i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}. Therefore
g(S)=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1} x_i.
Since g(S)=g, we get x_1+\cdots+x_{m-1}=g.

So x\in K_{m,g}. This defines a map
\Phi:\{S: S \text{ numerical semigroup with } m(S)=m,\ g(S)=g\}\to K_{m,g},
\Phi(S)=(x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}).

Now we construct the inverse map. Let x=(x_1,\dots,x_{m-1})\in K_{m,g}. Define
w_0:=0,\qquad w_i:=i+m x_i\quad (1\le i\le m-1),
and set
S_x:=\{w_i+qm: 0\le i\le m-1,\ q\in \mathbb N_0\}.
Equivalently, S_x is the set generated by the arithmetic tails starting at the w_i.
We prove that S_x is a numerical semigroup of multiplicity m and genus g.

First, S_x\subseteq \mathbb N_0 contains 0, because w_0=0.
Also m=w_0+m\in S_x.

We next prove closure under addition. Take arbitrary a,b\in S_x. Write
a=w_i+pm,\qquad b=w_j+qm
for some i,j\in\{0,1,\dots,m-1\} and p,q\in\mathbb N_0. Then
a+b=(w_i+w_j)+(p+q)m.
So it is enough to show that w_i+w_j\in S_x for all i,j.

- If i=0 or j=0, then w_i+w_j is just w_j or w_i, hence belongs to S_x.
- If 1\le i,j\le m-1 and i+j<m, then by the defining inequality of K_{m,g}, x_i+x_j\ge x_{i+j}. Therefore
w_i+w_j-w_{i+j}=(i+m x_i)+(j+m x_j)-((i+j)+m x_{i+j})=m(x_i+x_j-x_{i+j})\in m\mathbb N_0.
Hence w_i+w_j=w_{i+j}+tm for some t\in\mathbb N_0, so w_i+w_j\in S_x.
- If 1\le i,j\le m-1 and i+j>m, then x_i+x_j+1\ge x_{i+j-m}. Therefore
w_i+w_j-w_{i+j-m}=(i+m x_i)+(j+m x_j)-((i+j-m)+m x_{i+j-m})
=m(x_i+x_j+1-x_{i+j-m})\in m\mathbb N_0.
So again w_i+w_j\in S_x.
- If i+j=m, then
w_i+w_j=(i+m x_i)+(j+m x_j)=m(1+x_i+x_j)=w_0+(1+x_i+x_j)m\in S_x.
Thus S_x is closed under addition.

Next we show cofinite. For each residue class i mod m, all integers of the form w_i+qm (q\ge 0) belong to S_x, so every sufficiently large integer in each residue class lies in S_x. Hence only finitely many nonnegative integers are missing from S_x, and S_x is a numerical semigroup.

Now determine its multiplicity. We already know m\in S_x. For 1\le i\le m-1, positivity of x_i gives w_i=i+m x_i\ge i+m>m. Thus no element of S_x in a nonzero residue class is less than or equal to m. Also in residue class 0 the positive elements are positive multiples of m, so the smallest positive one is m. Therefore the multiplicity of S_x is exactly m.

Now determine its genus. In residue class i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, the least element of S_x is w_i=i+m x_i. Hence the missing nonnegative integers in that residue class are exactly
i,\ i+m,\dots, i+(x_i-1)m,
so there are exactly x_i of them. In residue class 0 there are no gaps, since 0,m,2m,\dots all lie in S_x. Therefore
g(S_x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1} x_i=g.

Thus x determines a numerical semigroup S_x of multiplicity m and genus g. This gives a map
\Psi:K_{m,g}\to \{S: S \text{ numerical semigroup with } m(S)=m,\ g(S)=g\}.

Finally we check that \Phi and \Psi are inverse to each other.

- Start from a semigroup S. Its Apéry representatives are w_i=i+m x_i by definition of \Phi. The construction of \Psi from x produces exactly the set of all numbers w_i+qm with q\ge 0. But every element s\in S has a unique residue class i mod m; subtracting suitable multiples of m (which belong to S because m\in S) shows that s can be written as w_i+qm with q\ge 0, while every such number lies in S because w_i,m\in S. Hence \Psi(\Phi(S))=S.
- Start from x\in K_{m,g}. In S_x, for each i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, the least element congruent to i mod m is exactly w_i=i+m x_i, since all smaller numbers in that residue class are the listed x_i gaps. Therefore the Kunz coordinate recovered by \Phi from S_x is exactly x. So \Phi(\Psi(x))=x.

Therefore \Phi is a bijection between the set of numerical semigroups with multiplicity m and genus g and the set K_{m,g}. Consequently their cardinalities are equal:
N(m,g)=|K_{m,g}|.
This is exactly the claimed statement.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2 and let g be an integer with g >= 0. Define K_{m,g} to be the set of all tuples x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers such that x satisfies the Kunz inequalities for multiplicity m, namely: for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}, and such that x_1 + ... + x_{m-1} = g. Then N(m,g), the number of numerical semigroups of multiplicity m and genus g, is equal to the cardinality of K_{m,g}.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix integers m and g with m >= 2 and g >= 0, and define K_{m,g} as in the statement.

We will show that K_{m,g} is finite.

Let x = (x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}) be any element of K_{m,g}. By definition, each x_k is a positive integer, so for every k in {1,\dots,m-1} we have
x_k >= 1.
Also, again by definition,
x_1 + \cdots + x_{m-1} = g.

From positivity and the fixed sum g, each coordinate is automatically bounded above by g: indeed, for any k,
x_k <= x_1 + \cdots + x_{m-1} = g.
So every x in K_{m,g} satisfies
x \in \{1,2,\dots,g\}^{m-1}
when g >= 1.
Therefore K_{m,g} is a subset of the finite set \{1,2,\dots,g\}^{m-1}, hence K_{m,g} is finite.

It remains only to consider the case g = 0. If x were in K_{m,0}, then each x_k would be a positive integer, so
x_1 + \cdots + x_{m-1} >= m-1.
Since m >= 2, we have m-1 >= 1, so x_1 + \cdots + x_{m-1} >= 1, which cannot equal 0. Hence K_{m,0} = \varnothing, and therefore K_{m,0} is finite.

Thus in all cases K_{m,g} is finite.

Note that the inequalities involving i and j are irrelevant for this finiteness argument: the positivity of the coordinates together with the fixed sum already places K_{m,g} inside a finite ambient set.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Let A and B be finite sets, and suppose there exists an injective function f : A -> B. We must prove |A| <= |B|.

Because A and B are finite, there exist natural numbers n and m such that |A| = n and |B| = m. We will show n <= m.

Consider the image f(A) = {f(a) : a in A} subseteq B. Since f is injective, the map f regarded as a function from A onto f(A) is bijective: it is surjective onto f(A) by definition of image, and it is injective by hypothesis. Therefore A and f(A) have the same cardinality, so
|A| = |f(A)|.

Now f(A) is a subset of B. Since B is finite, every subset of B has cardinality at most that of B. Hence
|f(A)| <= |B|.

Combining the two equalities/inequalities gives
|A| = |f(A)| <= |B|,
so |A| <= |B|, as required.

This proves that for all finite sets A and B, if there exists an injective function f : A -> B, then |A| <= |B|.

assembly_findings.description: The assembly relies on Lemma lem_20260324013805_2c445eb6 to supply an injective map J_{m,g}: K_{m,g} -> K_{m,g+1}. That lemma's proof is missing (empty). Without a demonstrated injective map, the application of the finite-set injection principle (L6) is unjustified and the final inequality N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1) is not established.

decomposition_findings.description: The decomposition cleanly isolates the genus-raising step as an explicit combinatorial lemma, which is good practice; however that lemma is critical to the final inequality and must be proven. Otherwise the decomposition is appropriate and no unused lemmas remain.

lemma_findings.description: Statement asserts existence of an injective map J_{m,g}: K_{m,g} -> K_{m,g+1} for all m>=2,g>=0, but no proof is provided. This lemma is essential for the assembly; lacking its proof the overall argument is incomplete.

result_payload.summary: Overall the decomposition and assembly are coherent and the lemmas/formal objects are consistent, but the crucial existence-of-injection lemma (lem_20260324013805_2c445eb6) has no provided proof. The assembly depends on that lemma to conclude the cardinality inequality, so the final step is unsupported until that lemma is established. No other large-scale circularities or definition mismatches were found.
